listenings.text: The first thing I stopped doing was the one I was best at, which I think is usually how it goes. I used to schedule the whole floor myself, every week, and I was quick at it because I had done it for eleven years. I handed it to a supervisor and the first month was worse. Not a disaster, but worse, and I had to sit on my hands and let it be worse, because if I had taken it back at that point I would have taken it back permanently. What I did instead was change what came to me. I still have the schedule sent to me on Friday, and I read it, and about once a month I ask a question about it. That is the whole of my involvement now. The thing nobody tells you is that the hard part is not handing over the work. The hard part is the six weeks after, when you can still do it faster than the person doing it.

I get called in when a company has grown and the person at the top is still working sixty hours, and almost every time the diagnosis is the same. It is not that they have not delegated. They have delegated a great deal. What they have not noticed is that the decisions keep coming back up, one at a time, disguised as questions. Somebody arrives at the door, asks whether they should do A or B, gets an answer, and everybody carries on believing the work is theirs. Nothing about that exchange looks like a failure. It takes ninety seconds and it feels helpful. But the deciding was the job, and it has just been handed back. What I ask a director to do for two weeks is not to stop answering, because that is unfair, but to answer with a question. What would you do. Nine times out of ten they already know, and about the tenth time you have found a genuine escalation, which is exactly the one you wanted to see.

paras: Ask anybody who built a company what the hardest part of growing it was and very few of them say money. What they say, in one form or another, is that they had to stop doing the thing they were good at. The founder who knew the machines has to hand the machines to somebody who knows them less well, and watch the first month go worse than it would have gone. There is no version of this that feels responsible at the time. It only looks obvious later, from the other side of it.

The pattern that keeps companies stuck has a name in operations circles: reverse delegation. A director hands out a task, the person hits something they are unsure about, they bring it back with a question, and the director answers it. Nothing dramatic has happened, and everybody in the room believes the task is still delegated. It is not. The decision came back, and the decision was the job. Do that ten times a week and you have a director with a great deal on their plate and a team that has learned, correctly, that the safest thing to do is ask.

The companies that get past it tend to change two small things rather than one big one. They separate the task from the accountability out loud, so that the person doing the work knows they own the result and not just the doing. And they set a rule about what comes back up: a genuine escalation is welcome, a question that the person could have answered is not. It sounds harsh written down. In practice it is the opposite, because the alternative is a team that never finds out what it is allowed to decide.
